summary: Rand's status report for the May 1971 meeting, answering RFC 116. It says software on the Rand IBM 360/65 was being updated for the new network protocol of RFC 107 and that a test logger was being built. No Telnet was planned until a specification was widely accepted.

eli5.summary: One site writes in to say how its work is going: we are fixing our software, building a practice tool, and waiting for the last piece of rules before doing more.

subtitle: Rand's May 1971 status report: updating its 360/65 software, building a test logger, and views on how the NWG should work.

tldr.problem: RFC 116 asked sites to report their status for the May 1971 Network Working Group meeting.
tldr.mechanism: Rand answers in three phases: current software and hardware plans, planned services, and comments on the goals and organization of the NWG.
tldr.outcome: Rand was updating its 360/65 software for the new NCP protocol of RFC 107, building a logger for testing, and planning to move to a PDP-10. It favored small working groups but not NWG-set long-range goals.

facts.label: Authors
facts.value: E. Harslem and J. Heafner, Rand

today: RFC 131 updates RFC 116, and its own status is listed as Unknown. It is a historical status report and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Phase One: The 360/65 and the Move to a PDP-10
sections.content:
Rand's 360/65 software was being changed to follow the new NCP protocol delineated in RFC 107, to finish before the end of May. A logger was also being built that, after an automatic ICP dialog, can be driven from a local console and send or receive EBCDIC, ASCII (8) or binary data. It is experimental, to let sites check out remote login procedures.

Rand had not planned a TELNET, but would implement server and user TELNETs, taking about two weeks, once a specification was generally accepted.

Rand plans to move to a PDP-10 and offer Network services there. The 360/65 connection would remain for some time, with maintenance for its lifetime but no new programs after September.
sections.eli5: The site is updating its old computer, building a practice tool, and planning to get a newer computer later.

sections.title: Phase Two and Related Activities
sections.content:
The UCSB/Rand work was reported in RFC 113 and earlier in RFC 78. Rand's Climate Dynamics Project would use it more heavily, and Rand built a front-end graphics program to show reduced data from UCSB as graphs, contours, plots and lists.

A working session on the Data Reconfiguration Service (DRS) had been held, with results to be published as an RFC. Rand also planned a position paper on a Protocol Manager, a software package allowing flexibility in experimental and production connection protocols, which should obviate a fixed logger on the PDP-10.
sections.eli5: The site is also drawing pictures from faraway data and thinking up a flexible tool that can speak many network languages.

sections.title: Phase Three: Views on the NWG
sections.content:
Rand favors the NWG as a forum, and small working groups and committees for particular specifications such as TELNET and the new NCP protocol, so long as no willing contributor is excluded. It notes the long lead time from forming a group to implementing its output. The NCP glitch cleaning committee is an example of expedient work, and UTAH had already implemented the new NCP protocol. Rand suggests guidelines on timely publication of reports.

Rand does not think the NWG should set the Network's long-range goals. The Principal Investigators have a better perspective, so the NWG Technical Chairman could host a one-day opinion session of them and report their views back for the NWG to turn into tasks.
sections.eli5: The site says small teams are good for making rules, but the grown-ups in charge should decide the big long-term plan.
